title: In Defense of Doing Things Together
author: James Tucker
source: Surfacing (jamestucker.substack.com); featured in EEDI 3-Read Friday #115, June 12, 2026
summary: James Tucker argues that the efficiency case for personalised, AI-driven learning is genuinely strong — and that this is exactly what makes it dangerous. Once efficiency governs schooling, the communal dimension of the classroom starts to look like a design flaw, and shared struggle gets reclassified as waste. Tucker distinguishes between children learning together and children learning the same thing together: the latter produces common ground — a shared stock of images and questions that travel between minds — and the experience of discovering that understanding is not private but worked out in public through confusion, comparison, and disagreement. Drawing on T. S. Eliot, Robin Alexander, Neil Mercer, and Michael Tomasello, he warns that 'cognitive sovereignty' — the capacity to hold, test, revise, and own your thinking — grows badly in a world forever adjusting to your preferences, and that personalised learning increasingly resembles the For You feed. Schools, he concludes, should protect shared texts, questions, and struggles not because they are efficient but because efficiency is not the only thing education is for.
points: The strongest version of the personalised-learning argument is also the strongest argument against it: optimisation forces you to classify shared struggle as inefficiency, but shared struggle is not a design flaw.
Learning the same thing together creates common ground — a shared stock of images and questions that thicken understanding when meaning is negotiated between minds.
'Cognitive sovereignty' — holding, testing, and owning your thinking — develops through being wrong in public and surviving it, and atrophies in a world calibrated to your present preferences.
Personalised learning comes to resemble the 'For You' feed: friction removed, fewer people thinking about the same thing at once — a cost, not a feature.
Schools should use technology for practice, feedback, and access but protect the common life of the classroom, because the teacher's inefficiency is part of the point.
quotes: The trouble with every increase in efficiency is that it forces us, whether we admit it or not, to decide what we are willing to class as inefficiency.
It is whether there is value in learning the same thing together. Whether it matters that they wrestle with the same mathematical problem, the same historical event, the same scientific idea.

It is the experience of discovering that understanding is not only something one possesses privately, but something worked out in public, among other people, through confusion, comparison, explanation, and disagreement.
Robin Alexander, Neil Mercer, and Michael Tomasello all point, in different ways, to the same fact: understanding often arrives in company.
You learn intellectual courage not by producing finished answers, but by offering a half-formed thought, being wrong in public, and surviving the experience.
Push the logic a little further and personalised learning begins to resemble the modern For You feed.

Schools should protect shared texts, shared questions, shared explanations, and shared struggles, not because these are always the fastest route to a tidy graph, but because efficiency is not the only thing education is for.
